content.text: An order whose total including tax and delivery exceeds $25,000 requires Procurement Manager approval.
On order review for an over-limit order, the buyer sees the banner "This order exceeds the $25,000 spending limit and requires Procurement Manager approval.".

expected_answer.operand: This order exceeds the $25,000 spending limit and requires Procurement Manager approval.

content.text: On order review for an over-limit order, the primary action reads "Submit for Approval" instead of "Place Order".
Submitting an over-limit order for approval creates an approval request ID in the format "REQ-" followed by 5 digits.
Submitting an over-limit order for approval records the request status as "Pending Approval".
Submitting an over-limit order for approval records the requester's name on the approval request.

expected_answer.operand: requester name on the approval request

content.text: Submitting an over-limit order for approval records the order total on the approval request.

expected_answer.operand: order total on the approval request

content.text: Submitting an over-limit order for approval records the submitted time on the approval request.

expected_answer.operand: submitted time on the approval request

judgements.rationale: [risk_factors] Applied money because the threshold governs whether a high-value purchase may proceed; auth because approval by a Procurement Manager is an authorization gate; user-reach because every Buyer can encounter the rule; change-frequency because pricing, tax, and delivery calculations often evolve and can shift threshold routing.

[risk_factors] Applied money and auth because the over-limit banner is the user-facing signal of a blocked direct purchase pending managerial approval; user-reach because Buyers reviewing high-value orders rely on it; change-frequency because UI copy and review-state logic often change with approval-flow updates.

[risk_factors] Applied money and auth because the primary action swap prevents direct placement and enforces approval submission; user-reach because the main CTA controls the path every affected Buyer takes; change-frequency because checkout actions often change when order-review flows are revised.

[risk_factors] Applied money and auth because request creation is the durable artifact that enters the approval control path for a spend-limited order; user-reach because every over-limit requester depends on the tracking identifier; change-frequency because identifier handling and workflow integration are common change points.

[risk_factors] Applied money and auth because pending status is the workflow state that prevents immediate placement and routes the purchase for review; user-reach because all over-limit requests surface this status; change-frequency because approval-state models are often extended or refactored.

[risk_factors] Applied money and auth because the requester identity is part of the approval record for a controlled purchase; user-reach because request ownership matters to every requester and approver; change-frequency because workflow record fields and approval views may evolve.

[risk_factors] Applied money because the total is the value under approval control; auth because approvers rely on that recorded amount to authorize the purchase; user-reach because every over-limit request needs the amount displayed; change-frequency because total composition can change with pricing, tax, or delivery rule changes.

[risk_factors] Applied money and auth because submission time is part of the audit trail for a spend-controlled approval request; user-reach because request tracking is visible to requesters and approvers; change-frequency because workflow metadata presentation often changes with approval tooling.
